plantinga-basic-beliefs: A properly basic belief is one a person is rationally entitled to hold without inferring it from other beliefs or supporting it with argument. The idea challenges classical foundationalism, which restricts the legitimately basic to what is self-evident, incorrigible, or evident to the senses; Alvin Plantinga argued that this criterion is both too narrow and self-refuting, since it does not itself meet its own standard. On his reformed epistemology, beliefs such as the existence of other minds, the reality of the past, and belief in God can be properly basic when they arise in the appropriate circumstances from properly functioning cognitive faculties. The account thus aims to show that religious belief need not rest on evidential proofs to be rational.
fate-vs-free-will: Fate and foreknowledge name a cluster of problems about whether the future's being settled or known in advance is compatible with human freedom. If events are fated to occur, or if an omniscient God already knows what a person will do, it can seem that the person could not have done otherwise, undermining genuine choice and moral responsibility. Philosophers from the Stoics and Boethius through medieval theologians and modern thinkers have proposed various resolutions: distinguishing foreknowledge from causation, arguing that God stands outside time so that knowledge does not precede the act, or holding that freedom requires only acting from one's own will rather than the ability to do otherwise. The debate remains central to discussions of divine providence, determinism, and the nature of free will.
